title: Go Down, Moses
origin: African-American spiritual of the Exodus; printed as a contraband song in 1862 and carried worldwide by the Fisk Jubilee Singers

pd.detail: First printed in 1862 as 'Oh! Let My People Go: The Song of the Contrabands' (Horace Waters, New York) and published in 1872 in The Story of the Jubilee Singers: With Their Songs; long out of copyright in the United States.
pd.sourceEdition: Digital Tradition transcription in G minor, cross-checked against Alan Lomax, The Penguin Book of American Folk Songs (Penguin, 1964), which prints the same tune in E minor
pd.notes: This basis covers the MUSIC only; the words carry their own independent basis in each section's lyrics.pd. The traditional tune is encoded, not any later concert or jazz arrangement. Both source transcriptions raise the seventh on the 'let my people go' cadence, so that figure is deg 7 with acc 1 (F sharp in G minor); the descending run in the refrain uses the natural seventh, which is deliberate.

notes: Common time throughout, no meter reduction needed. Both the verse and the refrain end with the tune's one-beat pickup (deg 5 below the tonic) on the last beat of the section, so any section can hand off into any other without dropping the famous upbeat.

pd.detail: Anonymous African-American spiritual text, taken down among the contrabands at Fortress Monroe and first printed in 1862; no identifiable author, in wide circulation well before 1900.
pd.sourceEdition: Theodore F. Seward (ed.), Jubilee Songs: Complete, as Sung by the Jubilee Singers of Fisk University (Biglow & Main, New York, 1872), cross-checked against Religious Folk Songs of the Negro, as Sung on the Plantations (Hampton Institute Press, Hampton, Va., 1909)
pd.notes: The 1862 contraband sheet ('Oh! Let My People Go', Horace Waters, New York) answers each call with 'Oh! let my people go'; the shorter 1872 Fisk wording is what is transcribed here, and it is what this melody encoding follows.

lyrics.notes: Stanzas 1 and 2 as printed in the 1872 Fisk collection, which carries four; its stanzas 3 and 4 are omitted for length, not for content -- nothing in this text is offensive. Stanza 1 line 3 was read from the 1909 Hampton printing, whose vocal underlay is legible where the 1872 engraving is not. Each line begins on the downbeat of its bar; the one-beat pickup that carries the first syllable sits at the end of the preceding section.

stanzas.text: When Israel was in Egypt's land
Oppressed so hard they could not stand
Thus saith the Lord, bold Moses said
If not I'll smite your first-born dead

pd.detail: Anonymous African-American spiritual text, taken down among the contrabands at Fortress Monroe and first printed in 1862; no identifiable author, in wide circulation well before 1900.
pd.sourceEdition: Theodore F. Seward (ed.), Jubilee Songs: Complete, as Sung by the Jubilee Singers of Fisk University (Biglow & Main, New York, 1872), cross-checked against Religious Folk Songs of the Negro, as Sung on the Plantations (Hampton Institute Press, Hampton, Va., 1909)
pd.notes: The 1872 Fisk engraving reads 'ole' in line 3 and 'Egypt land' in line 2; the 'old' and 'Egypt's land' of modern hymnals are later regularisations and are not used. The 1909 Hampton printing gives line 2 as 'Egypt's land', so both readings are attested well before 1930.

lyrics.notes: One stanza: the refrain is sung the same on every occurrence. Lines 1 and 3 are the call, each answered over the two bars that follow. Transcribed from the 1872 engraving, not from the modern singing wording.
